findings.claim: countPending() and create() run as two separate queries without a transaction or lock, so concurrent POSTs from the same user for different addresses can each read a count below the pending limit and all insert, letting the pending-request cap be exceeded. The partial unique index only prevents duplicate addresses and does not enforce the count limit.

The down() migration re-adds the full UNIQUE (space_id, requested_by, address) constraint, but a user who had a request rejected and then re-requested the same address (a flow this PR allows) will have two rows for that key, causing ADD CONSTRAINT to fail when rolling back.

The new rate-limit guard has no test coverage: address-book-requests.controller.e2e-spec.ts does not configure a rate-limit override or assert a 429 response, unlike the sibling address-books.controller.e2e-spec.ts which tests this pattern with initApp({ rateLimit: { max: 1, ... } }) and .expect(429).

Because the unique index is now partial (status = 0), a request for an address that was already approved no longer blocks a new proposal for that same address, allowing repeat proposals that approve() silently overwrites the existing contact's name and chainIds via upsertMany in address-book-items.repository.ts.
